input:
Pilot-scale testing plays an essential role in the development of carbon capture processes, providing data under realistic conditions before any commitment to larger installations. This passage reports a test of an amine absorption unit operated on gas from a cement kiln. The test extended over 60 days, processing 14 t of carbon dioxide per day.

During the test, the unit captured 87% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.9 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 2.1 kg per tonne captured. These results indicate that the unit was able to sustain a high capture rate over the test period while consuming steam and solvent at the rates stated, offering encouragement for the further development of the process.

Nevertheless, some caution is warranted when interpreting the findings. Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested, and it remains possible that dust accumulating in the solvent over a longer period could alter its performance in ways that the present test could not reveal. Additional long-term testing would be beneficial in order to address this uncertainty and to build a more complete understanding of solvent behaviour over extended operation.
target:
Capture reached 87% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas in a pilot amine absorption unit run on gas from a cement kiln. The unit treated cement-kiln gas throughout. The run lasted 60 days at 14 t of carbon dioxide per day. Steam demand was 3.9 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 2.1 kg per tonne captured.

Steam and solvent are both stated per tonne captured, and both figures are reported as measured, on the run as a whole. The basis matters for comparison: a unit capturing a smaller share of the gas can show a lower steam figure per tonne treated while using more steam per tonne actually captured, and the per-tonne-captured basis is the one that prices the product of the unit. On that basis the run's two consumption figures stand together, each stated for a tonne of carbon dioxide taken out of the kiln gas.

The claim closes at the run's edge. Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. Dust enters with the gas throughout the run, and the exposure within the run showed in the reported figures only as far as they go; solvent condition after longer exposure, and any rise in solvent loss that follows from it, are outside what this test states.
